With no work now in his grasp, he placed the knuckles of his right hand in the cup of his left, then those of his left in the cup of his right, and next drew a hand over his bearded chin. He repeated these movements in orderly succession, never pausing for an instant. To bring him back from the wandering state into which he invariably slipped after speaking was like rousing a person of extreme feebleness from a faint, or attempting to detain a dying man’s departing spirit in the hope that he might reveal something.

“Was it my name you asked?”

“Indeed it was.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Nothing more?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

Uttering a tired sound, neither sigh nor groan, he stooped to his task once more, until somebody again disturbed the silence.

“Shoemaking is not your trade?” said Mr. Lorry, regarding him steadily.

His hollow eyes moved towards Defarge, as though he wished to pass the question on to him. Finding no assistance there, they fell to the floor before returning to the man who had asked it.

“Shoemaking is not my trade? No, it was not my trade. I—I learned it here. I was my own teacher. I requested permission to—”

He drifted away again, for minutes together, continually performing the same measured movements with his hands. At length his gaze slowly returned to the face it had left. As his eyes settled there, he started and went on, like a sleeper newly awakened and taking up some topic from the previous night.

“I requested permission to teach myself, and after a long time and with great difficulty I obtained it. Ever since, I have made shoes.”

He reached for the shoe they had removed from his hands. Still fixing his eyes upon him, Mr. Lorry said:

“Monsieur Manette, have you no recollection of me?”

The shoe fell on the floor, and he remained seated, staring intently at his questioner.

“Monsieur Manette,” said Mr. Lorry, resting a hand on Defarge’s arm, “have you no recollection of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does no former banker, no former business, no former servant, no former time come back to you, Monsieur Manette?”

As the prisoner of so many years gazed fixedly first at Mr. Lorry and then at Defarge, signs long erased of a keen and purposeful intelligence gradually emerged in the centre of his forehead, piercing the dark mist that had descended upon him. The cloud covered them again; they weakened; they disappeared. But they had shown themselves.

It was after two o’clock when I suddenly turned and found myself beside the lake, near a cove where a small boat was moored. Our house was close by, and I could see my father and aunt walking on the lawn. I jumped into the boat and, well used to such things, pushed away from the shore and rowed across as fast as I could. My father has often told me how I looked as I approached: dressed in white beneath my tartan wrap, my hair flowing over my shoulders, and the boat moving faster than anyone would have expected me to make it go. He said I seemed more like a spirit than a human girl. As I reached the shore, he held the boat steady. I sprang lightly out and was in his arms a moment later.

Now my life truly began. Everything around me changed from dull sameness into a bright scene of joy and delight. The happiness I found with my father went far beyond even my most hopeful expectations. We were always together and never ran out of things to discuss. He had spent his sixteen years away among peoples almost unknown in Europe. He had travelled through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, entering the homes and settlements of local people with a freedom few Europeans enjoyed. His accounts of their customs, his stories, and his descriptions of the landscape filled hours with pleasure whenever we tired of discussing our own plans for the future.

Affectionate words were so new to me that I listened with delight as he described his feelings for me through those long years when he had seemed to forget me. “At first,” he said, “I could not bear to think about my poor little girl. Later, as grief faded and hope returned, she was all I could turn to. In cities and deserts alike, her small, fairy-like figure, as I imagined it, was always moving before my eyes. The cool breeze from the north seemed sweeter and gentler because I felt it carried something of your spirit. I often thought I would return at once and take you with me to some fertile island where we could live in peace for ever. On the journey home, so many fears struck down my eager hopes; the pain of waiting became almost unbearable. I dared not imagine that the sun might shine and the moon rise over your grave instead of over you alive. But no, that has not happened. I have my Mathilda, my comfort and my hope.”

Mary never wrote to Bath herself. The entire burden of maintaining a slow and unsatisfying correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Not long after breakfast, Captain and Mrs Harville and Captain Benwick arrived. They had arranged to join them for a final walk around Lyme. They needed to leave for Uppercross by one o’clock; until then, they intended to stay together and spend as much time outdoors as possible.

As soon as the whole group was out in the street, Anne noticed Captain Benwick moving towards her. Their conversation the night before had evidently encouraged him to seek her company again. They walked together for a while, discussing Mr Scott and Lord Byron as before. They were still as incapable of agreeing precisely about either poet’s merits as they had been the previous evening—or as any two readers might be. Eventually something caused almost everyone in the group to change companions, and Anne found Captain Harville at her side in Benwick’s place.

“Miss Elliot,” he said, lowering his voice a little, “you have done that poor fellow a kindness by getting him to talk so much. I wish he had company like yours more often. I know being shut away as he is does him no good, but what can we do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” Anne said, “I can readily believe that would be impossible. But perhaps, with time—we know what time can do for every kind of grief. And you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend’s mourning is still quite recent. It was only last summer, I understand.”

“Yes, that’s true enough,” he said with a deep sigh. “Only June.”

“And perhaps he did not hear of it immediately.”

“Not until the first week in August, when he returned from the Cape, having just been appointed to the Grappler. I was in Plymouth, dreading any word of his arrival. He sent letters ashore, but the Grappler had orders to sail to Portsmouth. The news had to follow him there—but who could tell him? I couldn’t. I would as soon have been hanged from the yardarm. Nobody could do it except that good fellow.” He pointed to Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had reached Plymouth the week before, and there was no danger of her being sent back to sea. He risked everything else. He applied for leave, but without waiting for an answer he travelled day and night to Portsmouth, immediately rowed out to the Grappler, and stayed with the poor fellow for a week. That is what he did. Nobody else could have saved poor James. You can imagine, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us!”

Anne had no difficulty imagining it. She said as much as her own feelings permitted, or as his seemed able to bear. He was too deeply moved to return to the subject, and when he spoke again it was about something entirely different.
